newsitem.title: USA: NYS blasts Giuliani's budget for 'ominous' gaps.
newsitem.headline: NYS blasts Giuliani's budget for 'ominous' gaps.

text.p: New York State's Comptroller on Tuesday said the Giuliani Administration was frittering away a windfall produced by Wall Street banks and brokerage houses, and failing to close large, future budget gaps.

"While the city's fiscal year 1997 outlook is much improved, largely due to windfall profits from Wall Street, the report questions the use of this revenue for spending increases and tax cuts, rather than paying off debt or reducing out-year gaps that are still ominously large," said H Carl McCall in prepared remarks.

McCall, whose report comes on the heels of criticism voiced by the city comptroller, Alan Hevesi, estimated that the city would have a $391 million surplus in fiscal 1997. This was at the high-end of the range of $220 million to $396 million that the city official forecast.

And the state official saw about $2 billion of risks in the city's fiscal 1998 budget, pointing out that the Giuliani Administration might not collect the $600 million of state aid that it was counting on from Albany's cuts in Medicaid and advance revenue-sharing.

Other risks highlighted by McCall included the city's expectation that Albany lawmakers would give extend the $12.5 percent personal income tax surcharge, which expired at the end of 1996, on an "unqualified" basis, and plans to sell the mid-town Coliseum convention center and collect back airport rents from the Port Authority, an issue now being arbitrated. In total, he saw $1.4 billion of worrisome, one-shot maneuvers in the mayor's 1998 plan.

And McCall predicted the city would have to search for more risky gimmicks in the years ahead because it was failing to deal with long-term problems. Among the potential problems identified in the report were a plan to raise wages without capturing productivity gains, the cost of rising debt service that could have been reduced with the fiscal 1997 surplus, and the possibility the mayor's 3.4 percent spending increases could soar to 7.6 percent if revenues fall short.
